utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. For the record, I just note that we start late today in order to give the accused some time for his preparation of his examination, because he couldn't have access to the internet or the e-court from the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. We appreciate the Chamber accommodating us for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. Good morning, to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Subotic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I asked you about the number of those who were released from Keraterm and Omarska. On page 45 yesterday, Mr. Tieger suggested that there were thousands of Muslim civilians who were detained in our prisons. Can you tell us about our policy towards civilians of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the policy of the state leadership, there were no plans about any prisons at all. The policies were such that what happened during conflict and during combat was considered to be -- how should I call it? That's how things happen in wars. There are prisoners, there are wounded, there are killed, and so on. In other words, those who are imprisoned are stationed or kept in some buildings, in company buildings, in schools and barracks on both sides. And now this is what I could say about the state policy because that's what I know, and now how that functioned in practice is an entirely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the instructions and orders that arrived from the office concerning civilians and their rights?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions and orders were those that were prescribed in the Law on National Defence, and that was done very precisely and very clearly. The law prescribes everything correctly and precisely. In every sense, I and the government, the ministries and so on insisted on the compliance with the law. Nobody can deny that things were done in that way. However, a war is a war. People can do all sorts of things. Some observed the regulations, some didn't. I'm sure that there were some problem there, that there were mistakes made, but when it comes to rules and regulations, and when it comes to the state leadership, everything was clear. Because of those mistakes and because of those regulations, there were some discords, we have already discussed that, and I already mentioned a lot of those in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 46, Mr. Tieger quoted from a letter from the Ministry of the Interior and referred to the Crisis Staffs and some units of the army who were requested to collect as many civilians to be exchanged. What was the position of the minister about those requests? Did the police met those requests? Did the police meet those requests? On the page 46 of the transcript, you cannot find it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the transcript from 2006?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, that's yesterday's transcript. Mr. Tieger quoted from a letter written by the Ministry of the Interior, and in that letter he says that that's what was requested by the MUP. Did the minister support that or did he raise his voice against it? Did the MUP comply with those requests?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How could the witness answer the question without seeing the letter? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's also a mischaracterisation of the quote from the report of the July 17th, 1992. Dr. Karadzic said -- anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Mr. Tieger did not display the letter. He only read one part from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But then if you'd like to put a question, you should read correctly. Let us see the letter then in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just for purposes of responding to that, I mean, Dr. Karadzic can either quote back accurately what was put to the witness previously or show the document itself. He did neither.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that Mr. Tieger did not mention the document number. He quoted from it. Page 46: [In English] [As read]The army Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslims as -- Muslim units as possible and delete [phoen] them." [Interpretation] And so on. This should be P1096. However, Mr. Tieger never mentioned the number. Maybe he would like to call it up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is mentioned explicitly on page 40123 of the transcript at line 11.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My page numbers are different. Your Excellencies, I would like to have the same page numbers, and I would like to be able to upload from my room. I'm really totally incapacitated. I'm in a very unfavourable position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is in the same position as well. The page numbers are being updated the next day. That's my understanding. There is no problem if you refer to by your page number, 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, more to the point, it was mentioned in exactly the same spot where that quote is mentioned. It's not just going to occur on some later page that can't be found so that the -- I made the page reference here so everyone would know where it is, but it's right at the spot where the quote was -- was -- was made so it's -- it's -- there's no difficulty in knowing that it was P1096 and in not asserting the day afterward that no citation was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you read that line, Mr. Tieger said at the 17th Assembly session and that by way was P1096. You should have it on your page as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 46 I don't have it. There is no citation. There is no exhibit number. Could I now call up page 4 in the Serbian version, page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, look at the first paragraph from the top of the page. This was quoted to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is page 3, but it is page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says the army and the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. How do you understand the position of the Ministry of the Interior about these requests?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me for a moment while I read this. I understand it in this way: The minister of the interior - I was in the government at the time so I remember - he opposed that. He criticises the army, Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies, and he says that they have requested to round up or capture as many civilians. The minister of the interior says that the conditions in some of these camps are poor. There's no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the following page. Look at the second paragraph where it says it was pointed out --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was pointed out that the priority of the national and crime prevention services is detect [as interpreted] war crimes, provide documentation, on-site investigation, photos, expert testimonies, medical findings, and file criminal reports. Documents are also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this tally with what you know about the position of the government and the ministry about these issues?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. Both things are correct and were correctly put by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 8 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document was put to the witness originally because of his assertion that he had no way of knowing how many people were in camps, so he's directed that particular part of the report. Now Dr. Karadzic appears to be using the report generally for various purposes in a leading fashion. So before we turn to this part of the report and the witness is directed to some portions of it which the accused will presumably ask him to affirm or not, we should know exactly how this arises from cross, what the witness's information is about the subject that may be at issue, and only then turn to portions of the report as it may be necessary as is -- as has been repeatedly emphasised to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Let us collapse the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give up on the further examination about the document, but it was pointed out that the witness affirmed such treatment of civilians. The general was a minister in the government, and I would like him to be able to see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you move to another topic, please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll change topic. I'm giving up on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, there was a lot of talk about Koricanske Stijene. May I be allowed to ask you whether during the summer of 1992 the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina continued under the chair of Cutileiro and Carrington and did I attend those conferences?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where I was from the 21st to 29th August 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you were in London. I don't know whether I'm right, but I know that you were somewhere abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the two of us talk to each other during that time? Were you in Krajina before the 30, before I returned, and then on the 30th we went there again together? When did you visit Krajina for the first time to discuss Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when you arrived at Pale. I can't remember the exact date when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you establish that the military had nothing to do with that? Under whose authority was that incident after that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established that at the meeting in Banja Luka. As far as I remember, it was Sunday. A meeting was organised involving all the protagonists - let me not enumerate them: The police, the prosecutor's office, the judiciary - that meeting took most of the morning. They reported to me about those things very correctly, and then the entire team went to the site to look at what we could see. However, there was nothing special for me to see there. In any case, I transferred or I passed on the duties and tasks. At that meeting I learned that the army was not involved at all. Nobody even mentioned the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From then on under whose authority was that matter?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the case was taken over by the judiciary, the investigating judiciary teams and so on. I returned on that same day to Banja Luka and then on to Pale, and I submitted a report as to what I had done. I had made notes at the meeting, and I also submitted those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that there were actions or efforts to cover up some parts of that crime?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that. In the part that I participated in, there were a lot of people involved from various institutions, so nobody could sweep anything under the carpet. It could not be covered up. They put in place measures. They organised actions, and all those actions were done after my departure. I no longer participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if an investigating judge was involved, whether investigators were involved, whether forensic experts were involved? At that meeting was it ever mentioned who was supposed to be involved?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was mentioned. I don't remember the names of the judges in question, although I knew some of them. In any case, it was said very precisely at that place who was supposed to do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there indicia, was there evidence, were there indications that Simo Drljaca had either ordered them or allowed them to do what they did?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that place at that time at that meeting, I did not learn anything concretely. I did not note any such thing. What Mr. Tieger said yesterday is true and that is that it was said at the time that there were three people who were the main protagonists of the whole situation, that they had left what Mr. Tieger said yesterday. Let me not try and find the exact quote. I adhere by that, because that's what I noted at the meeting. How -- how accurate that was, whether it was true or not, I can't be a judge of that because I didn't have any information to that effect. That was all the information that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 15, but then I have this new page numbering. After 78 again I have 1 in terms of yesterday. That was some mention -- or, rather, you asked about pressure, and you said that Republika Srpska was exposed to pressures exerted by international factors every day. Can you tell us whether this pressure proved to be justified or, rather, founded on some truth?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Throughout the war this propaganda was really something that could not be proven, but we in Republika Srpska could not do anything about that or against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the responses of our services? Actually, did we check what the international community would send by way of some kind of objection or information?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did check for the most part, and always -- I mean, I know and I have quite a few things written down. Your talks with Akashi, in particular, and so on and others too, in terms of Professor Koljevic, that convoy, et cetera. Always there were inaccuracies there. It was all sort of muddled. It was always the army that was blamed and Republika Srpska, as if -- well, although the army on several occasions found ammunition and other things. There were all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A letter was shown asking for access to detained persons in Srebrenica. Did we have a prison in Srebrenica before or after the fall of Srebrenica? Did we have a prison for anyone in that area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know we did not have a prison, but -- I mean, I did not hear of us having a prison there, so I cannot guarantee 100 per cent that there wasn't some - how do I put this? - some situation when these people were brought together in certain areas so they would not be directly involved in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, but let me go back to the previous question. Your answer was that we asked for checks. What did our services tell us in terms of the accuracy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic. Where did the witness say the Serbs asked for checks?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 20. Page 9, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Subotic, yesterday when asked by Mr. Tieger, that you said there's -- you said you are not aware of such pressure, and you could not discuss it. Do you remember having said so? Shall I read out what you said? "Mr. Tieger, the international community was pressuring Republika Srpska every minute, every moment, and you are asking me now to split hairs. I was always under pressure, not just myself but everybody in Republika Srpska. How could I have known about every instance of pressure by the international community? These pressures were there every day. So I will tell you what I know sincerely. I'm not afraid of anything. But don't impose any mention of any pressure on me that I'm not aware of it. There's no reason for that. I'm not aware of this. Therefore, I cannot discuss it." Having said so, how could you now talk about a check that was done on your part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I carried out checks. It was organs of the army, organs of the MUP, then those teams of Professor Koljevic's and so on. It's not that I took part in these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why did you not answer so yesterday to the question of Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the way I've said now. There's a wish to explain this more precisely. As for this question that Karadzic put to me, this was done by different people so I do not have that specific information that I could present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, perhaps it's my fault for this confusion. I'm not asking you about any specific case today. I'm asking you about this phenomenon of international observers raising certain objections. And then what did we do about that and these checks? Did they confirm such instructions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did not. Our people always said what it was that was not right there and what it was that was right. I know that. That's the way it was at all these discussions. So there was no reason -- well, however, this was because differences were pretty big between the claims made by these international factors in relation to what we were experiencing on the ground, the army, the humanitarian agencies, and others who were working on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When I asked you whether there was some prison in Srebrenica for those who were missing, I did not mean during combat and in the immediate aftermath. What I meant was during those letters, did we have any other prison in that area except for Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not that I know of. Not that I know of. I don't know whether there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Batkovic available to the International Red Cross whenever they wanted access?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, whenever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, but please put a pause between the questions and the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We apologise to the interpreters and to the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, please, could we pause. Could you tell the Trial Chamber roughly how many POWs did we have? How many people were taken prisoner in combat from the beginning of the war until the 10th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember -- I mean, some conversation. I actually have that written down in my statement too. About 20, or a bit over 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, quite frankly, I don't know exactly. For the most part they were tried, investigated. How all of that ended up, I don't know. To be quite frank, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there were any pardons that came from me in order to carry out exchanges even for those who had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that kind of thing. I don't remember to what degree, but this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there unilateral releases from our sides allowing people to go to third countries?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All of this was made possible for them. They could go to third countries. They had very favourable conditions. As far as I know, quite a few did go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for these exchanges, in addition to these pardons and unilateral releases, did the president's office deal with these simple exchanges? Whose authority was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had organs for exchanges of prisoners of war, and the president's office did not deal with that from that point of view. It was these organs that had been tasked with doing that. From time to time we did receive such information. At any rate, this was an organised effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of these 20.000 POWs approximately before July 1995, did you receive any information or documents or evidence that there were executions that would make it incumbent upon you to be careful with regard to each and every other situation when prisoners were taken?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of any such document, and I never saw any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there things that happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about directives. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of document a directive of the president of the republic is -- or, rather, of the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a strategic type of document. That is to say the uppermost type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happens to it once it returns to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand this question. Could you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does the Main Staff use it for? Is it directly implemented or what does the Main Staff do on the basis of that directive?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a directive is prepared in the Main Staff, and it is adopted in the Main Staff and it remains in the Main Staff. And on the basis of that directive, they have to organise operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these operations are ordered by which documents?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations are ordered through orders issued by commanders of corps, brigades, and so on. That is to say on the basis of what the Main Staff had sent to these commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, your answer was that you did not know why the directive was sent to the 1st Krajina Corps. In the light of what you told us just now, can you tell us what was supposed to be sent to the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order. A directive is not sent to corps. Only orders are sent to corps, different types of orders, orders for higher-level units and orders for lower-level units. Commanders of these units write these orders, that is to say commanders of these formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that directives are created in the Main Staff. Were there are directives that were not created at the Main Staff, but, rather, at the office, those that have to do with humanitarian matters rather than combat?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were shorter directives, and I think that there are such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a very leading question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As always, and he should be reminded of this, it continues to reduce whatever probative value the accused hopes to gain from this tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, who drafted the directives that were created in the Presidency and that were not combat related?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I created some of them. Some we worked on together, and people from other ministries took part in them, those that had to do with these events and these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please call up on our screens -- half of the screen, actually, P838, and the other half of the screen D104, in Serbian at that. And could the participants please refer to the translations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters do not have that possibility, so when you read the document, please read very slowly. I know P838 is a directive 7, but what is D104?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D104 is a directive. These are two directives that were created. Now we're going to ask the general where each one of them was created and in the drafting of which one he took part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this directive on the right-hand side, the office of the president to the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For the record, the witness is indicating D104, which is a directive of 11th of March, 1993. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. So to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I'm not going to read the letterhead, just the directive: "Directive, Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska shall in the future as well enable unhindered passage and protection for shipments, equipment and, staff extending assistance that is being provided to the civilian population of the other side. "2. Ban abuse for military purposes of food supplies --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, Mr. Subotic, please concentrate on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- answering the question. Mr. Karadzic asked you: Where was each one of these created, and in the drafting of which you took part. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you say where the directive on the right-hand side, D104 drafted -- was drafted? Who signed it? What's the protocol number? Who's stamp it is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the directive is from the office of the president of the republic. You signed it. The stamp is yours. Therefore, we created it in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the protocol? Whose is that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protocol is also from Pale. It's ours, dated the 11th of March, 1993, the cabinet of the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does the 01 indicate?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 01, yes. 01.87/93. I think that's the first directive as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Well could you please look at the same elements on the page to the left. Where was it created? Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Subotic, at one point of time you said in case of documents you drafted, the protocol number should be 02. Do you remember having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was just in reference to the stamp, 02. When I personally drafted a document, then the stamp used a 02. This stamp here is 01, meaning that it's the president's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were not involved in drafting of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did take part. I did. But the president directly signed it. When the president did not directly sign it, then the 02 stamp would be used, but the president would issue an order or would approve that I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this number 2 that you are talking about, where is it? When you sign it and send it, it would still be the president's office, but where do you see this 2?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the stamp. On the stamp. This is the Republika Srpska, the president of the republic, but then it would also say 2. That would be the number on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the letterhead on the left-hand side document to see where it was drafted, and what is the protocol number?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the number of the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska, dated the 8th of March, 1995, or it could be the 9th. I'm not sure. It's a little bit blurred here. It was sent to the command of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the IBK, the Herzegovina, the Drina, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Could we please look at the last page so that we could see the signature and the stamp on this document on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the document please be scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, can we look at one page but last. This is an attached or an accompanying document. And could we please zoom in on bottom part of the page?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp says "Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," and the signature is Supreme Commander Dr. Radovan Karadzic. This is what I said, that this was done in Han Pijesak, that it was drafted without my presence, and you can see that this seal, this stamp, proves it, and that I did not know about the directive or its implementation. This is 100 per cent proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So who was it then who drafted this? Was it the Supreme Command or --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by Main Staff, and they gave it to you to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at P4818, please -- 4481. The interpretation gave it to you is not quite precise.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means to trick. Perhaps there's another expression, "to plant," "to trick." Perhaps the gentlemen can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is written now in the transcript is not an issue. It's the answer -- it's not a question. It's an answer by the witness. The first and second sentences are by me, and then the rest of that is the answer of the witness. [In English] "It means trick and perhaps there is another expression ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A little bit earlier you were talking about what was happening with the directives. Are you able to tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned -- as far as I'm concerned as the chef de cabinet of the president of the republic, this document, as far as I'm concerned, is a document by the Main Staff. It's not a document of the Supreme Command or by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now look at this document issued by the Drina Corps based on the directive. Are you able to look at it? You were talking about orders and commands. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness just now said this is the document of the Main Staff? Did you say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a document of the Main Staff, because it has the stamp of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is talking about the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the previous one, the directive. Because no military document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- no, you said so already. We are now talking about this document which is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, you mean the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what it means order for active combat?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Zapovest" is an order which can encompass the brigade as the top possible level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page, please, item 2. In English it's page 3, and could you please read item 2 so that you can tell us what the gist is.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to directive number 7 of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone as soon as possible in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to reduce them to their urban areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us -- I think that you didn't read all the numbers. You said directive 7 and 7/1. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First line.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, first line. The first line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first line of item 2.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2, the command of the Drina Corps pursuant to operation, directive number 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah, all right. Thank you. So whose are these -- whose directives are these, number 7 and 7/1?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the directives 7 should be the directive that was drafted at the staff. 7/1 is now kind of amended directive, one that as soon as it's 7/1 means there's been some amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now get the one page but last in the Serbian and page 7 in the English. Are you able to tell us -- it's a little bit blurry, but it says "Security organs." This is the fourth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps page 5 is clean, but that is also --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can read it. Security organs and military police will indicate the areas for the Assembly and security -- and security --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 5 to the witness, please. It's -- it's much clearer. There should be another page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does this part arise from the cross-examination? What part of cross-examination are you dealing with now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the part that refers to the directives and their consequences so that we can see how these directives are worked through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The security organs and military police will indicate the areas for the assembly and security of prisoners of war and war booty. "In dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population, adhere in every way to the Geneva Conventions. "The security organs --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General, sir. In yesterday's transcript, page 4, lines 2 to 5, it was suggested to you that the text in the directive, direct 7, is illegal, and you agreed that that should not be in the directive. So how is it worked through further? How is this sentence developed further here? How does this paragraph fit into that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not fit in. This sentence does not fit in that other text, because this is proper and correct what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a little bit earlier that directive 7/1 must have had some kind of change. Can we look at paragraph P4226 -- actually, no. Exhibit P2246. Could we look at the English version, and can we zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can we zoom in a little bit? All right. Very well. Can we zoom in a little bit more to make the letters bigger? All right. That's good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us first when it was drafted and who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was drafted by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 31st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the next page, please. Can we zoom a little bit, please. I think it's page 3 in the English. Could you please read the task for paragraph 2, just the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Based on directive number 7, the Army of Republika Srpska has the task, first --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, General, just that. So could you say whether this directive stems from directive 7?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 5 in English and in Serbian. Can we look item 5.3, Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's very small. Can we zoom in on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you read 5.3, that paragraph, and read what is stated as the task for the Drina Corps. Can you please read it to yourself and then say whether that sentence that you said was illegal is there, whether it's being repeated here in brackets. Read it to yourself. Just read up to the end of that paragraph, up to 5.4.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is absolutely not a single word from that other text, and it has nothing in common with that other text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And so would that be that change, then, that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that is that change. This is written properly, and that sentence is not there. There isn't even a part of it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this directive 7.1, does it task the Drina Corps to capture Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just to separate, and there are specific tasks mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, now we will move on to the topic of the sessions of the Supreme Command. You were asked about that. In paragraph ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up P2242, but I'm not sure. Please bear with me for a moment. P22042, it is a diary that was kept by my secretary. Can we look at the entry made on the 16th of March, 1995. It is a meeting that you attended and that you already mentioned in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's page 33 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please look at line 2 under the 16th of May, 1995 -- or, rather, the 16 of March, 1995. In line 2 it says: "Between 11.0 5 and 15.0 5, Tolimir, Milovanovic, and Subotic were in the office." That's the second bigger part where Drago Simic is the first entry.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Drago Simic at 16.05. It says at 1100 hours, Tolimir, Subotic, from 11.05 to 15.05.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is the first person?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that. I found Tolimir and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before Tolimir. Before Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We collapse English for the moment and zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is excellent now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to explain what this is about. General Subotic. Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember Mira and Milijana who were the assistants to the secretary for Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you know they kept a notebook to maintain -- to arrange his agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know they put first minus or a hyphen and then when that was -- that appointment was implemented they put it into a plus or a cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A plus. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is Milovanovic, Tolimir, and Subotic. There was no other Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, this was one day after the directive 7 was sent to the 1st Corps. Can you tell us whether during that period of four hours what was discussed? What did the four of discuss during those four hours? What did we discuss? What were the problems at stake at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the problems were of the nature that can be found in the order by the Drina Corps. As far as I can remember, that's what we discussed the most, what needed to be done, and that's what we have just seen just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I don't follow your answer. You said: "... the problems were of the nature that can be found in the order by the Drina Corps." Could you expand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean we talked about that operation, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What operation? Did you mean the -- but I think that Operation Krivaja 95 was drafted some time in June or July, if my memory's correct. We are talking about March now, and we are talking about March 16th, and Mr. Karadzic pointed and told you that the day after -- on the day after, that is on the 17th of March, directive 7 was sent out to the corps by the Main Staff by General Milovanovic. Now, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now you remember what you discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Very well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, at that meeting did we read the directive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that meeting were there discussions to the effect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It's leading. I asked what the witness discussed with these generals together with Mr. Karadzic. Do you remember what you discussed? Your first answer was you discussed the operation of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that I see this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that meeting did we mention the creation of bad conditions for the population?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What population do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, I'm giving up on this. General, sir, in paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you leaving this topic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If the general does not remember what was being discussed during the four hours of the meeting - I suppose that there were a lot of topics that were discussed - in that case I'll give up on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have some questions with this. I take it, Mr. Subotic, that these generals are -- were meeting the president for four hours at the president's office. I take it it's a very uncommon happening. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be honest, I can't remember. This is what I honestly believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the meeting took four hours. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can say yes to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Generals speaking, meeting with the president for four hours is not a usual happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The discussion was probably lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we upload Exhibit D2149, English page 53, B/C/S page 35. Shall we show the witness the first page first. Mr. Subotic, this is what Mr. Milovanovic, General Milovanovic, wrote about his meetings with president between 1992 and 1996. And Mr. Milovanovic confirmed his writing. So shall we go to page 53 in English and 35 in B/C/S. So the bottom part of the B/C/S. So I read out for you: "On 16th March I had a meeting with Karadzic in Pale because of some documents that needed to be signed and which were made by the Main Staff operations administration for the purpose of the Supreme Command since they did not have people skilled for that." Do you see that document [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that, yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is it, a document that needed to be signed which were made by the General Staff, the Main Staff operation administration for the purpose of the Supreme Command. I take it this is the 16th of March where -- when you and Mr. -- General Tolimir and Milovanovic met with Mr. Karadzic for four hours, so I take it you discussed this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so. I can't remember. I should be shown some other details of that conversation. However, based on what I see before me, based on those few lines I can still not get to the bottom of what was discussed. If there is anything else, maybe it will jog my memory. As things stand now, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree that a president office or Supreme Command did not have people skilled for drafting military documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not agree with that. Only partly, only in some segments the answer would be yes. However, in most of the segments the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Thank you very much for those questions, but since you're able to ask leading questions and I think there is one topic that we just left out that ought to be asked, and that is: Was this language about making life unbearable for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa discussed at all at this meeting. I think that's an important element that ought to be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since the witness did not remember this conversation, I would rather leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. If you have any further questions you can do so, but not in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the general to read the last sentence on the page that's before him, and could he also be provided with the following page in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the page be scrolled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last on your side.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the letters be enlarged? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where it says the Supreme Commander criticises General Mladen Djukic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go on reading from there. Read the sentence aloud to the end.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "And Colonel Luka Dragicevic and a few other VRS officers because of our arbitrariness. I informed General Mladic about the criticism, but I don't know how they talked it over, if they did it at all. Because of my people, but also due to lamenting of the entire VRS, President Karadzic decided then to hold a session of the RS National Assembly and saw the supply problems and further engagement of the army. The Main Staff had to make an expose or report on the situation in the VRS and its needs and requirements and bring it up at the Assembly session sometime in mid-April." And now finally I remembered what we discussed. We discussed general problems, and a request was made to discuss it at the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when it comes to General Milovanovic, does he mention that we discussed directive 7?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was it the first time that you heard the sentence, and I quote, "Life has to be made unbearable for the population of Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much after Srebrenica. I don't know when. A few months after the events in Srebrenica. I didn't know what the directive contains. Only when some discussions started about all of that, it was only then that I -- and then I reacted as well. And now, today, after what I have just seen, I didn't have that. Now I'm 100 per cent convinced that that's -- that there was a deliberate alteration because the order issued by the Drina Corps doesn't mention that, and no corps has the right to change anything in the wording of the Main Staff. However, the wording of the Drina Corps document does not contain that sentence which makes me even more convinced that that was subsequently added and perhaps it was not even done at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 25 -- or, rather, 234, that's in your statement -- or, rather, that's your previous evidence where you mention that Srebrenica was discussed. You say the plan was to do this or that or the other. Can you tell us whether at that session the Supreme Command made plan? Was it discussed? Did any decisions follow?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No plans were worked out. It was only precisely outlined that those two enclaves should be separated from each other. I know that. I remember as much. I registered that in the minutes of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to call up P3149. It is something that you sent, the minutes of the session of the Supreme Command that you yourself did not attend. And that was shown to you during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the fourth session that I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see in e-court page 13 in Serbian and page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be cautious before we go to documents and place them in front of the witness. I recognise this document was discussed during the cross-examination, but it's a lengthy document. So I'd like to know -- and in particular in light of the fact that the accused referred to the witness's evidence in chief rather than any aspect of cross, I'd like to know how this arises from cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you agree that this document was raised in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was definitely raised in my cross-examination, but for -- as I say, it's a lengthy document. I don't know what point in particular is being raised here. And to give you an extreme example of the abuse of such a process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was about to answer the question. Please leave a gap. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, it was put to the witness that after all, Mladic did respect him, that he expressed his esteem and General Subotic's statement was disputed from that aspect, his relationship with General Mladic, that is. And this document contains explanations, so I wanted to ask General Subotic about that. However, we can deal with it after the break if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we take a break? We will resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, on page 17 on the 19th, on the 19th of June, you were asked, and now I'm going to read this out in the English language so that it would be properly interpreted to you: [In English] "Q. When did you first find out that there were executions of any sort that took place in Srebrenica?" [Interpretation] I'm not sure that on the 19th the word "pogubljenje" was used. I think the word "egzekucija" was used. [In English] "A. Sometime towards the end of July, the month of July, I was in Pale, I was in Banja Luka. I did not know a thing. I did not know a thing. I'm telling you honestly. Nobody ever informed me about anything. I was in the office. I didn't receive any report about that. "Q. Okay. So you said sometimes toward the end of July you found out about executions that had taken place, and then you told us what you didn't know about or didn't or weren't informed about. What were you informed about toward the end of July concerning execution of Bosnian Muslims? "A. Well, I was informed that Muslims, and I saw it on TV, that Muslims were provided with buses to go to Tuzla. I was also informed that Naser Oric, and I knew that already that Naser Oric had killed a significant number of Muslims who did not agree with the things. That's what I knew, and I had that kind of information. Not just me. That was generally known. I didn't see anything. I was not in the area. I was not duty-bound to go there." [Interpretation] And then on pages 17 and 18 something was quoted to you, Mr. Milinic's testimony, that is, and he said that he had not heard until much later. In this part of your answer where you said what you heard, again I have to repeat Mr. Tieger's question to you, when was it that you heard that Serbs executed prisoners in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but I heard that in Banja Luka when I was watching television and I saw them boarding buses and some other vehicles. That's what I saw on television in Banja Luka, and that was commented upon. So I was not in that area, so I didn't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which television was that, and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did they say -- actually, first of all, in 1995, in July, did you receive reports from the Main Staff that were sent to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I mean, at that time, no, I was in Banja Luka. I was there, and Mr. Micic, your Secretary-General. We had some assignments there. So at that time we saw that in Banja Luka. I mean, we heard this information in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's the television?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which television was it when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on Serb television, I think, this relocation, the Muslims moving. I saw General Mladic there giving children something, whatever. It was on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, that is beyond dispute, but this is what I'd be interested in: Did you receive any reports or did you find out in some other way about some Muslims being executed or unlawfully killed? Not killed by Oric, but, rather, killed by the Serb army? Did you hear of that, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. When I returned to Pale, I did not receive that kind of report, and I didn't find a report when I got back either. Such a report did not exist in our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to see in these reports that were sent by the security organs of the Main Staff to the Presidency was there any information to that effect, that the Serb army had executed someone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to the session of the Supreme Command, and please, could we -- yes, we do have that document. We've called it up. It's your document P3149, and you are sending these minutes, and then Mr. Tieger said to you that at this meeting Mladic said that he respects you. So could we please have page 12 in e-court in Serbian, and I think it's 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I don't have the page number here, could that please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what was put to you, this is what you were asked on the 19th, on page 77, lines from 5 to 19, I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Q. Do you agree in general that in this portion of the Supreme Command session that was held on 31st of March, 1995, General Mladic indicated his understanding of Mr. Karadzic as Supreme Commander, his position as Dr. Karadzic's right hand, and also offered a generous or fair assessment of you, at least not a hostile or hateful assessment." [Interpretation] And now please take a look at this page that we see here. Could we enlarge the bottom of the Serbian page, please. Karadzic says: "I cannot be the law, but I cannot operate outside the law. "General Mladic: None of us can be the law, and we cannot be the law individually. Don't say things to us. We know what you want with that. "Karadzic: Tell us what it is that I want. "Mladic: I won't tell you what it is that you want. I know what you are trying with that. I know --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we on the correct page in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's at the top of the page: [In English] "So you are telling me what I want." [Interpretation] That is not the right translation. "Well, tell me what it is that I want," that would be the right translation. And then it says that this has to do with the suspension of the authority of the Main Staff in connection with promotions. They tolerated that for you until now, but from now on we will see if we continue like this, we will have to clear some things up, and then further on I say: "Do Bogdan Subotic transfer that authority to you?" And Mladic says: "General, in relation to -- as far as I'm concerned, Bogdan Subotic is not a person who should be mentioned in my presence." And Mladic says: "He was your choice for minister." And I say: "And it will always be my choice for as long as I am who I am."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these expressions of respect for you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under quotation marks, because Mladic thinks that he is the smartest man in the world, that he's smarter than I am and that you are, and the prime minister, and that no one else knows anything, and that is how he treated me all the time. I never responded to him. You know that full well. And there is no record of me standing up to him in any way. I simply tolerated it. It's the kind of person he is. As a matter of fact, I think that often he didn't really mean what he said. Quite simply, he had this position -- I mean, he would be angry, whatever, and he had to blame someone for something. I never accused him, to tell you the truth. I never entered into any kind of polemic with him. That's a well-known thing. You know that, but others know that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but you did withdraw from the post of minister.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I was not minister any longer, but this conversation took place three years later almost. I mean, now three years later, why would he mention all of that? All of that was stated very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 18 in Serbian and 20 in English.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say 18 in the Serbian? I can see page 19 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's all right. It's in e-court. You can see line 6 here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please indicate where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start over again and let us know where it is in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Fifth line from the top, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "This is what we military men have been brought to, whether craftsmen or generals. He can be arrested at Subotic's decision. We have no idea, only when we hear that he was arrested. Did he commit a criminal offence? It turned out that Vlatkovic had not been doing anything. Karadzic: But who did? Someone comitted a criminal offense. Sorry, I do not know. I do not know who should be arrested, and now when we are with Subotic, where did Subotic get such authority? Who empowered him? In whose name was he in power? Does he have operational powers? He cannot appear as a general."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can't follow with that speed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Ah, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do not know who should be arrested, and now when we are with Subotic, where did Subotic get that authority? Well, we can all read that, and then Karadzic says: "Everyone is empowered to make a criminal report, everyone. Everyone who knows about a crime is duty-bound to make one." And then a bit lower in my answer I say the military structure cannot do civilian jobs nor can the civilian structure do military jobs. That is very elemental. And if we are not going to respect that, we will introduce chaos to the country, and we will lose the country. And then again Karadzic says: "The Main Staff is the operational body, as the police are located in the Interior Ministry but are not interior ministry." And then I say: "The army must go to the ministry in the same way that the police goes to the ministry." Did you know about these positions of mine about the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's just some story going around. Mladic's problem was that there was somebody there who had the right to oversight, and even though I lost the right of oversight over the army, I remained until the end of the war with the right to the oversight of other state organs. This is something that was never abolished. And as the inspector in chief, this is what my main task was. It says to determine and check measures established by law for the defence of Republika Srpska. That is the first assignment. The second assignment is to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I initially thought that the witness was reading from or reciting something from memory or reading off the screen but he's referring to some document, some small document he has in his hand, and reading from that, so I think we need to know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my identification as chief inspector, and it's there in the documents, but I did bring it, but this is in the documents. It's contained in the documents. So I had four assignments. I read the first one, if you noted it down. The second one is to establish the system of command. That is something that I was doing in that year, and since Mladic asked the president for me to stop monitoring the army, I didn't do that anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, do you remember what the question was from Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember the question, but Mladic disputes all of that here in this conversation. He places an anathema on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you -- could you concentrate on answering the question put by Mr. Karadzic, and if you would like to refer to something, please let us know. You are free to consult any document you have with you now, but please let us know in advance. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I believe that we already have that in the statement. I'm just asking you this: This position of mine that the police should be in the Ministry of the Interior and that the armies in the Ministry of Defence was something that was proper and correct and based on the law, and did I manage that implement that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was correct and proper. I really couldn't give you the percentage to the extent to which it has successful, but in any case, it was not quite successful. It wasn't fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger mentioned your paragraph 169, I think, where I think you -- and he mentioned that you said that there was a letter in which President Milosevic bypassed Karadzic and promoted Mladic. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He sent a letter also to Alija Izetbegovic and - wait, let me see to who else - and to Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 15459 and on the other side can we look at 15461, both are Serbian versions, and they can follow the English version on their monitors. Can we zoom in on this, please. Could we have 15461 on the right side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the two letters I mentioned. On the left-hand side is the letter to Alija Izetbegovic. I don't know if I ought to read it. And then on the right-hand side is the letter to General Ratko Mladic, and there is no mention anywhere of the president of the republic, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first sentence from the Mladic letter?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am addressing you and the Main Staff. It says General, sir, I'm addressing you and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and thereby the leadership of Republika Srpska at the moment in time when all the absurdity of the civil war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina is becoming obvious and when, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Can we look at the last pages of both letters so that we can see when it was signed and who signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter sent to Izetbegovic was sent from Belgrade on the 1st of August, 1995, and there is the signature of Slobodan Milosevic and his signature, and then it says CC or attachment letter sent to General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can we look at the last page of the document on the right-hand side, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sheet needs to be scrolled up a little bit. A little more, please. Otherwise, the signature is probably on the next page. The one on the right-hand side, the one to the -- to General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's lost somewhere. You can see the ERN number at the top.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, General, sir, how was this taken, this double letter in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking it was a sorry affair. First of all, Serbia did not do much to help us, neither did Slobodan Milosevic, and then with this letter they actually did us a disservice, especially -- well, this is a strange thing for everybody. It was unnecessary and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you know, did you find out, did you establish if there was any kind of and what sort of joint criminal enterprise there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before going into that question, I don't follow that this is a "double letter," because it's impossible to see the English translation at the same time. What did you mean, Mr. Subotic, by "double letter"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say that in this address to Alija Izetbegovic, I wanted to say what does Slobodan Milosevic mean in addressing Alija Izetbegovic at the end of the war when we were losing territories en masse? The whole world was against us. What does that mean? What is that then? And he's not addressing the president of the republic, but he's addressing the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina who started the war. And then on the other side here, he is vilifying the president of the republic and placing his weight behind Ratko Mladic, who at the time was planning a coup d'etat against Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what does a "double letter" mean at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'm afraid that it was I who said that in my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, two letters were sent, one to Alija Izetbegovic, one to Mladic. In that sense, it's -- there are two letters. The one to Alija does not excite us, and it does not -- didn't mean anything to us, but the one to Mladic, it really got us into a state, and it did mean something to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The contents are different, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course they're different, because the situation is different, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on, because I was confused because you compared -- tried to compare these two letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can you just please tell us what would the normal procedure be? How should it have been in Republika Srpska? Who would be the counterpart, the partner to Izetbegovic in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should have been addressed either to the government or to the president or to the Assembly, one of those three segments. If it had been written to any one of those, then it would have been all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
