utterances.text: Thank you. I put a question, but then there was this clarification afterwards. General, sir, throughout the whole time that you were dealing with state and administrative affairs, did you come across any evidence or knowledge that there was any kind of joint criminal enterprise on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Court has already expressed its position in -- with similar attempts by the accused to ask such broad conclusionary, legalistic and inappropriate questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us hear the question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, throughout the whole cross-examination regarding the elements, it is understood and implied in my charges that he entered into a joint criminal enterprise with many people including Mladic, including President Milosevic, including the opposition, for example, Seselj and so on, that I joined that enterprise in order to commit crimes. Did you know of the existence of any kind of joint criminal enterprise of that type?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. That's a kind of legal assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Then we'll do it like this: Was there any agreement? Did you find out about any agreement between myself and anyone else about the commission of any kind of crime?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing like that. It did not exist. I absolutely state that no one in our republic ever thought about anything like that, never mind found out or established it. I personally think that this is some kind of made-up thing, criminal enterprise, because that is the first time in the history of human warfare and human living, life, that I ever heard of anything like that, and I tried with some very intelligent, wise people to get them to explain it to me, and nobody could do that. It's a very unclear thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So any kind of agreement like that, any kind of commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No kind of commission of crimes. I'm not aware of anything like that. If anybody else knew anything like that, then they would need to prove it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say anything after the answer of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just thanked the witness. My question was: Was there any kind of agreement in order to commit crimes, agreement between myself and anyone else, and I think that the witness answered that question. And then I also said that I would like to tender these two documents. Perhaps that's what it was, and that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive them separately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3718 and D3719 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, do you know when this letter to Mladic was sent by President Milosevic? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the date is here on the letter, Belgrade, August 1st, 1995, and that was sent to Mladic then also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was a letter to President Izetbegovic. I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the same time, in 1995 when the initiative was started for the replacement of Mladic, that's when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, sir. I have no further questions for you, and I would like to thank you on behalf of the Defence for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Subotic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for the professionalism of this Trial Chamber. I'm absolutely satisfied for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton will be coming in, probably is coming in now. While she's doing so, can I raise one housekeeping matter dealing with MFIs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They -- this relates to two MFI documents that needed a translation and now have one that I understand has been uploaded. It's P6394 MFI, and 6395. So both the English and B/C/S have been added in e-court, so I would ask now that they be fully admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will take a look and issue an oral ruling. Does the Defence take any position with respect to these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't oppose it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Probably you heard this advice from the Mladic Chamber, but I have to repeat it for record. Mr. Salapura, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a Rule that we have at this Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a -- as a consequence you refuse to answer question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you -- in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Salapura?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you, and I would like to remind myself because I'm the main culprit here, that you make a break after my question and that both of us speak slowly so that our words may be recorded properly. Colonel, sir, could you please tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of August, 1948, in Bjelaj village in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac in the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your father's name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although that is already in your statement, could you please tell us something about your career path. In addition to what is already in your statement, can you tell us whether you were ever decorated or awarded?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mention some of your decorations, when you were decorated, and by whom? Was that while you were still in the JNA or later?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: My decorations mostly date back to the period of the JNA. While I served in the VRS, I only got one decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not outdo ourselves it seems. Thank you, Colonel, sir. Did you provide my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to call up 1D9615 in e-court. Could you please look at the screen and tell us whether this is the statement that you gave to my Defence team. It should be on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D6273 will be Exhibit D3721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 1D6274 will be Exhibit D3722.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a summary of Colonel Petar Salapura's statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before Dr. Karadzic begins the summary. If he could have a look at the very last sentence of paragraph 6. I can't find any evidence to that effect in the statement, so perhaps he could just couple check that. And on the printed-out copy I have paragraph 6 begins with the road from Belgrade to Han Pijesak so the last sentence I don't think is something that comes from his written evidence, although I stand to be corrected if I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If necessary, then maybe ask the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, do you have your statement before you in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The summary. I thought that this referred to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have the statement before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Trial Chamber will allow you to have it before you and to use it during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Colonel please be provided with a copy of his statement. And now I'm going to read the summary in English. [In English] Colonel Petar Salapura worked in the JNA until 1992 and then joined the VRS until his retirement in 1996. He was head of the administration for intelligence in the VRS Main Staff. In May 1992, the leadership of Yugoslavia withdrew the JNA from BH and the VRS was formed. The VRS inherited the organisation of the JNA. After the JNA withdrew from BH, Petar Salapura's intelligence organ was organised within the VRS. The intelligence organ was given the task and the right to deal with the Patriotic League of the Army of BH and the Croatian Defence Council. The security service did not provide them with any information which put them in a difficult position. The situation was also influenced by changes in other departments. They were exposed to the attacks of Muslim paramilitary formations against Skenderija. They also had great trouble with public opinion. They were blamed for not doing anything in Croatia. Petar Salapura proposed that a department of administration be formed at the administration for intelligence and security. The AIS was established, and the chief of the administration was Colonel Tolimir, Colonel Petar Salapura was chief of the intelligence department, and Colonel Beara was chief of the security department. In 1994, the AIS split into two administrations, the security service and intelligence administration. There were personnel problems. None of the departments in the corps had more than three men. Half the intelligence work at the strategic level was done by Colonel Petar Salapura. General Tolimir dealt with staff co-ordination and contacts with the commander. The intelligence department was not as significant as the other powerful, strong, and often rival services, interior counter-intelligence services. The intelligence service gathered intelligence in the war about the enemy, the terrain, the facilities, and everything pertaining to the enemy, but also about the overall activities, plans, intentions of the international community, relations, upcoming conferences, concluded agreements, et cetera. The intelligence service had no jurisdiction over internal matters. The service operated twofold. One part was the intelligence administration with organs for data collection and the intelligence centre. The other made the unit part, these were organs in the staff of the corps, brigades, et cetera. Colonel Petar Salapura's jurisdiction in the intelligence administration was very limited. In July 1995, Colonel Petar Salapura was chief of administration. At the time, the intelligence service focused on co-ordination and collecting intelligence pertaining to operations and events, which would ensure in the Serbian Krajina and the western part of Republika Srpska. The focus of intelligence was -- work was transferred to the western part, to Croatia, the BH Army, HVO, and the Croatian forces in Dubrovnik. There were indications that Croatia was preparing offences against Krajina and Republika Srpska. They received initial information on the joint attack on the Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska from intelligence services in Belgrade. The road from Belgrade to Han Pijesak was cut off due to the fighting in the area on 12th and 13th of July, 1995. It was impossible to contact General Tolimir that day or the following. Petar Salapura went from Bijeljina to Han Pijesak via Zvornik, Nova Kasaba, Milici, and Vlasenica. In Nova Kasaba, Colonel Salapura spoke with Major Malinic. There were a large number of captured soldiers at the stadium. The situation was quite relaxed. Prisoners were sitting and walking about the stadium. One could not fathom that anything could happen to jeopardise the prisoners. On the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac, a group of those who surrendered were left on the side of the road. One of the prisoners activated a grenade, causing delays. There were several tens of soldiers and prisoners. In Bratunac there were many vehicles moving in all directions. There was a great deal going on. There were many civilians there. Petar Salapura explained the situation to General Mladic in Srebrenica. They discussed the -- the expected attack. As soon as combat operations against Srebrenica started, the monitoring of intelligence transferred to the Drina Corps. The 65th Motorised Protection Regiment was not linked to the intelligence administration. They secured the prisoners at the stadium in Nova Kasaba. The 10th Sabotage Detachment was an independent unit, a headquarters support unit of the Main Staff. Professional control training, specialist training, proposal of use for reconnaissance task, activities in the territory of the enemy, were conducted by the intelligence administration. Anything outside professional control could not be ordered or interfered with by intelligence officers. The intelligence administration had nothing to do with Operation Srebrenica in July 1995. Liquidation of prisoners was never considered at the Main Staff. No one ever conveyed such an order. The administration considered the liberation of Srebrenica unnecessary, because of the expected negative reactions of the international community. In June 1995, the administration planned and the 10th Sabotage Detachment executed a pre-emptive action in Srebrenica. They wanted to avoid civilian casualties, but through restrictive actions they demonstrated that they could enter the town whenever, but it was not in their interest. This was a message to the Muslim forces leadership in Srebrenica and UNPROFOR as support to exert pressure against the Muslim side to stop premeditated provocations against the VRS. The aim was to make it impossible for Muslims to carry out constant assaults, attack Serbian settlements and the VRS carry out provocations and inflict losses. And that would be a summary. At the moment I would not have any questions for Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salapura, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing, that is, your written statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. May I just correct one thing, if you will allow me? The 10th Sabotage Detachment was not a logistics unit. It was an independent unit of the Main Staff. It was directly subordinated to the commander of the Main Staff. The administration was an organ for professional control of the detachment, its training, equipment, and it proposed its use to the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, we're not going to be sitting for much longer today, but I know you have a bad back and you've been sitting all morning, so if it becomes too much to stay sitting, I do invite you to let us know; all right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, this is the fourth trial that you've testified in in front of this Tribunal; right? You've testified as a Defence witness in the prosecution of Blagojevic, and as a Prosecution witness in the case against General Tolimir, and as a Prosecution witness in the trial of General Mladic, and that makes this the fourth proceeding you've come to give evidence in; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in 2011 you also testified at the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the trial of members of the 10th Sabotage Unit for the killings at Branjevo Farm on the 16th of July, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you explained in your statement that General Tolimir, as chief of administration -- of the administration for intelligence and security in the VRS was your superior. Now, you know also that after the trial where you testified, he was convicted of genocide and extermination for the murder of Bosnian Muslim men and boys from Srebrenica, among other things, and sentenced to life imprisonment. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Colonel Beara, who you explained was the chief of the security administration and your counterpart, was convicted in 2010 of genocide, murder, extermination, and persecution and also sentenced to life imprisonment for his role in the killing of the men and boys of Srebrenica. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I want you, to begin with, to go over with me, if that's okay, some of the evidence you gave before another Chamber of this Tribunal yesterday and today while it's still fresh in your mind. And I'm going to read to you what you've said and ask if you can confirm that for us. The first thing I want to turn to is yesterday, at transcript page 13102, and this is in respect of the killings in Srebrenica, you were asked by my colleague, Mr. Vanderpuye, he asked you, and I'll quote: "Did you not report this crime because you knew that other members of the Main Staff were fully aware of it, both how horrifying it was and of its scale and who committed it?" And then His Honour Judge Orie asked: "Or was it that the other part of the question or was it that you had no obligation to report?" And your response was: "Yes, it's correct. I heard there, as well from my operatives that I talked to. Everyone knew. I think even the whole town knew about it, let alone the army. So I thought that it was a process that was underway." And then Judge Orie further asked you: "Let me try to see whether I correctly understood your answer. Do you intend to say that there was an obligation to report but that there was no need to do that any further because everyone knew already? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?" And you said: "Yes. I believed everyone knew, and when I received it, when I talked to my operatives, yes." Does that accurately reflect --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt you finishing your question, but, Mr. President, we don't have access to this. This is a situation where because of the Rule 75 procedure we receive access to Mladic case on a very delayed basis, and so we don't have access to this material, so I would ask that we be given access over the weekend and that she ask any questions about the transcript or Mladic on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any difficulty postponing the remainder of your question in relation to Mladic evidence to next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: None whatsoever. My only interest in doing it now was while it was fresh in the colonel's memory, but of course not. And we can e-mail the transcripts to Mr. Robinson immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And then deal with this and then let's move on. If you have -- Mr. Robinson, if you receive by e-mail, you have no difficulty with proceeding with this part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: With this question, yes, but we would like to -- if they have any other questions on the Mladic testimony then on Monday after we've had a chance to review the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just deal with another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether witness has answered the question. Whether you asked a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't, but perhaps maybe it's best in all the circumstances just to go to another area in the time we have remaining to give Mr. Robinson a chance to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you follow that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, but if you allow me, may I just say something? Today we discussed it again. I asked for the recording to be listened to again to make certain corrections in the interpretation or whatever it was. So we agreed this morning precisely on this and what all of this meant, or, rather, all, because there were mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so, and I was watching that and I wanted to go over that with you in totality, but what we'll do is we'll do it on Monday; all right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to go to another area, I just want you to confirm for me Monday of this week you went out to meet with Dr. Karadzic at the gaol; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I noticed that one of the things you added to your statement, and it was in paragraph 23, which is at page 26 of the English and page 17 of your language, was that you had only met Dr. Karadzic three times during the war and had no recollection of ever speaking with him on the phone, and you said the same thing during your testimony in the Tolimir case. Now, Colonel, when you talked about it in the Tolimir case, Mr. McCloskey showed you Dr. Karadzic's appointment calendar for 1995, and he explained to you that we'd received evidence that if there was a plus mark next to the entry in the appointment calendar, that means that it happened. And I want to go to Dr. Karadzic's appointment calendar, which is P2242. Now, you saw during your testimony in the Tolimir case a reference - and we could go to page 9 in both languages - a reference that you had spoken to -- with Dr. Karadzic and the 18th of January, and you were scheduled to meet him on the 24th of January. And do you see, Colonel, third up from the bottom on the 18th of January, reference to you, your name for five minutes? That's what the entry reads: "Call Professor Koljevic," with a plus sign, and then another plus sign with what looks like a telephone exchange number, 42-243-074, Colonel Salapura. So you see that; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm looking for it. I'm looking for it. Is it on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps if my colleague could enlarge the entry that's --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Oh, I see the part written this hand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- thank you. Now I'm going to show you a couple of entries from that book. In your Tolimir testimony you saw that you were scheduled to meet with Dr. Karadzic on the 24th of January, and in this book, if we can go over to page 15, the entry for 30 January, you see here that somebody by the name of Mico Pusic advises Dr. Karadzic that he should call you, and I'm going to take you to a few more entries and I'm going to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go over to page 16, I think, of this document, the entry for the 1st of February. And I'll have to go over to my own e-court to tell everyone where it is in English because I don't see it in Cyrillic script at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think page numbers are identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This -- this says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we go to the English page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please. So for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, this is the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1st of February on the English page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here, seven up from the bottom we see that you spoke with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We may collapse the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because the entry with your name has got a plus sign beside it. And then if we go further over in this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Edgerton, did you say Mr. Salapura met Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I hope I said spoke with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I said spoke with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we go over to pages 25 of this book in both languages, it looks like if you go down to the entry of 28 February, you spoke with Dr. Karadzic's brother, Luka, who passes on a message to that effect, saying that you spoke with him. And then if you go over to page 27 in both languages, the entry for 4 March 1995, you see your name. And that's your extension, right, third up from the bottom? 226, that's your extension number. And that shows --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That shows you spoke with Dr. Karadzic on the 4th of March. And I won't take you to the next page in the book, but I'll tell you that there's also an entry that says you called his office - at page 117 in both languages - on the 26th of September -- pardon me, the 28th of September. And it wasn't only for 1995 that we see that you spoke with Dr. Karadzic. If we have a look at P4368, which is Dr. Karadzic's appointment book for 1994, and if we go to page 12 in English and page 19 in B/C/S, we should see an entry for 16 February 1994. And that shows that you called Dr. Karadzic's office with a message to contact somebody named Zerar who has something important to say. If we go over to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The English page is not appearing as you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, page 19. I spoke incorrectly. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Make sure that Chamber and other people are following. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English page 12; B/C/S page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 16th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we go over, please, to English page 15 and B/C/S page 23, and if we go to the entry for 22 February, we see your name again sort of halfway down that entry, and your exchange, 226. So Dr. Karadzic spoke with you again on 22 February, 1994. And if we can go over to English page 40 and B/C/S page 69. It's a bit difficult to decipher the date here, but that's an entry for 21 May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence, please, for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this shows that you met with him and 21 May. And I'll just tell you at English stage 98 and B/C/S page 180, you and he made contact on 14 November 1994. And I'd like to go over to a new document, please. That's P1484, and it's the notebook of General Mladic, and I'd like to go to English page 53, B/C/S page 57. It should be an entry dated 13 December 1993. I think I might have read you the wrong B/C/S page number again. Your indulgence for a moment please. The B/C/S page reference is 53. And my apologies to you as well, Colonel. Colonel, this entry in General Mladic's notebook records a meeting in Belgrade with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic, General Milovanovic, General Djukic, General Miletic, General Maric, you, Mico Stanisic, Tomo Kovac, and for the Serbian authorities President Milosevic, General Perisic, Jovica Stanisic, and Frenki Simatovic. And I haven't showed you all Dr. Karadzic's notebooks that record meetings with you, Colonel, but on the basis of that I've shown you alone, we see many more contacts with Dr. Karadzic than just three. So you told two Trial Chambers about only three contacts with Dr. Karadzic, and my question is: Are you trying to hide the number of contacts you've had with him, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Direct contacts, that's what I meant, what I remembered from that distance. It's a different thing when we met up sort of all together during the war. Well, I mean even now. Even now if I were to enumerate all of that, I couldn't. There were shorter encounters, longer ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I mean, really, I have no reason to conceal any one of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement? You received your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you ever the last page, paragraph 23? Could you read out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war I met with President Karadzic only three times. I do not recall ever having talked to him on the telephone. I never informed -- never informed President Karadzic about execution of prisoners in writing, nor did I discuss that with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you admit that you spoke to Mr. Karadzic over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see here that there were telephone conversations -- or, rather, whether they were materialised or not I don't know, but I'm talking about the three meetings I had with him directly at my request now. This was -- yes, yes. All right. Yes. Okay. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second sentence in that paragraph. Is -- now you remember that and you admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, and I see that. I cannot say. I do not recall these meetings. To this day I do not recall them, but I accept that. I see it's there on paper, so that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for -- stop here and adjourn for today. Mr. Salapura, probably you are aware of this, but please do not discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving testimony, testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something about the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do it on Monday. We'll continue on Monday at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of June, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
